sources: Triumph NL (new): 14 current models. The specification page is server-rendered (seat height, torque, power EC) and the Cloudinary image assets carry the model year in their file name ("my26"). Images hotlinked from the maker's page, never copied.

KTM NL (new): 21 current models. The page title and URL name the model year ("2024 KTM 1290 Super Duke GT"), the og:image is the maker's dated asset, and the technical-specifications page gives seat height, torque and weight without fuel (stored as dry weight, never as wet weight).
Honda / Suzuki / Yamaha NL (re-run): 54 pages, prices and year-stamped images refreshed; the stale Suzuki V-Strom 800 / 1050DE records that produced the 112.6 hp figure were retired.

Wikimedia Commons: a year-targeted search pass ("Yamaha MT-07 2021" etc. for the last three years of each generation) over every family with 300+ registrations, followed by a category-tree walk with a parent-category fallback. Both throttled to Commons' Retry-After (45–58 s), one job at a time.
German Wikipedia: refresh of every known article after the power parser was rewritten to read the figure next to its unit ("80 PS (59 kW)" was read as 80 kW before).

Not usable: kawasaki.nl (client-rendered, no model pages in the sitemap; the US, EU and UK sites redirect or 404 from here), bmw-motorrad.nl/.com (connection refused), cfmoto.nl (page has no model images), vespa.com/piaggio.com (bot-blocked). Their generations still depend on Commons and German Wikipedia.
weak: Kawasaki and BMW have no official source. Z900, Z650, Versys 650, Ninja 650, R 1250 GS, R 1300 GS, F 900 R/XR, S 1000 RR/XR all depend on Commons or German Wikipedia photos. Where a generation carries a dated photo it is eligible; where only an undated family photo exists on a divided family it stays out of discovery by rule.
Manufacturer images are hotlinked, not stored. If a maker moves an asset the card loses its image and falls back to a Commons photo or to none. The importer re-checks on every run.
Seat height and torque are still mostly absent for makers without an official page or a German article; nothing was inferred.
Availability is NEW only when the maker's current listing says so or the last admission year is current; a bike still sold but missing from the curated page table can show as USED.
Registrations are RDW first-admission counts by type code and remain the only weighting. A type code shared across variants (e.g. A2 and full-power versions) is counted once for the family.
verdict:
How much of the real modern market would you see? A round limited to generations sold from 2020 shows 338 generations carrying 60.5% of all Dutch first registrations of modern generations (Audit II: 52.9%). Among the 48 generations with 1,000+ registrations, 31 are in (64.6%); of the Top 100, 69. The 31 Top-100 generations still out carry 43,886 registrations, 21% of the modern market.

What important is missing? The gaps are not random. They cluster on two makers whose sites cannot be read from here and whose Commons photographs are undated: Kawasaki (Versys 650 both generations, Versys 1000, Ninja 1000SX, Z1000, the 2025+ Z900) and BMW (R 1250 GS Adventure, the single most-registered modern generation, and the S 1000 XR). The Suzuki 650 twins (V-Strom 650, SV650) are out because Suzuki NL no longer lists them and their dated photographs are of earlier generations. CFMOTO is absent entirely (450MT, 800MT), as is the Vespa GTS. Several previous generations of bikes that are in (MT-07 2018–20, MT-09 2017–20, Tracer 9 2017–20, Ténéré 700 2019–24, Tracer 7 2020–24, CB650R 2019–23, Tiger 900 2020–23, 790 Duke, 1290 Super Duke R) sit out because only their successor has a dated image; that hurts a used-bike search more than a new-bike one.

Is a Top 5 unlikely to be materially biased? Not in general. For a buyer of a new bike the answer depends on the segment. Big adventure and sport-touring above €15,000 is well covered (R 1300 GS and GS Adventure, Africa Twin and Adventure Sports, Multistrada V4, Tiger 1200, V-Strom 1050, NT1100, Tracer 9, 1390 Super Adventure) with the 1290 Super Adventure S and Versys 1000 missing. Middleweight nakeds are well covered (MT-07/09, Z650, Z900 2020–24, CB750 Hornet, GSX-8S, Street Triple, Trident, 790/990 Duke) but the current Z900 and Super Duke R are out. The middleweight twin-cylinder adventure/all-rounder segment under €12,000 is biased: Versys 650, V-Strom 650, SV650, 450MT and 800MT are all absent while Tracer 7, NC750X, Transalp, V-Strom 800DE and Tiger Sport 660 are present. A Top 5 there would be a Top 5 of what could be photographed, not of the market. Anything Kawasaki- or CFMOTO-shaped in your taste will be under-represented; anything Honda, Yamaha, Suzuki (800+), Triumph or KTM will not.

What the numbers are worth. Every figure on an eligible card carries its evidence status; nothing was inferred to reach these numbers. Two things changed in this pass that make the values more honest and the coverage figures slightly lower than they could have been: a maker's page now describes only the generation its model year belongs to (the 2016–2020 NC750X no longer wears the 2026 power figure), and a German article that opens with a 1970s machine of the same name no longer supplies a modern bike's power. Six power conflicts remain on record, all with the registry's figure shown.

failureNotes.Harley-Davidson Street Glide Special: Commons search found two 'FLHXS' files; both were dated to other years of a six-way detected family. The family's boundaries are detected from registry steps, so undated files cannot be placed.
